Issued at 200 PM EDT Thu Aug 6 2026

As southwest to southerly flow continues the rest of today into 
tonight ahead of an incoming cold front, expect the sunny skies 
today to allow temperatures to bring highs into the upper 70s to mid 
80s, with observing platforms already showing temperatures generally 
in the 70s to lower 80s (warmest in the downslopes by Lake 
Superior). With mostly clear skies continuing into the overnight 
hours, expect temperatures to drop down into the 50s across the 
interior areas, with fog potentially returning to the south central 
once again late tonight. Ahead of the cold front on Friday, expect a 
near repeat of today, with highs again in the 80s, warmest along the 
Lake Superior downslopes in the central and east. While on the 
warmer side, generally pleasant weather is expected the rest of 
today to Friday (at least before the cold front arrives); take some 
time to enjoy the outdoors or get some outdoor work done. However, 
come Friday, be sure to keep an eye on the forecast and sky as the 
cold front moving in could bring rain showers and thunderstorms, 
beginning in the west by no later than the afternoon hours.

Impactful weather returns to the U.P. on Friday as a cold front 
starts to push into the area. While 0-6 km bulk shear isn't all that 
impressive along the cold front (only around 30 kts), with models 
trending the cap weaker at around 850mb, convection could become sfc-
based by the afternoon hours. Thus, we may see SBCAPE/MUCAPE at 
around 1200 to 1500 J/kg by the afternoon to early evening hours 
over the west half. In addition, with strong theta-e advection lined 
up well with cold frontogenesis in the lower to mid levels, thinking 
there will be robust mechanical lift along the front to produce 
strong updrafts to support linear convection Friday afternoon. This 
is generally supported by the varying CAMs; while there is still a 
range on the timing on when the front arrives (could be as early as 
the morning hours, but highly doubtful of it), the general model 
consensus is that showers and storms move in during the mid-
afternoon hours (2-4 PM EDT). Thus, while generally not expected 
along the line, a strong thunderstorm or two could bring some 
marginally severe winds (i.e. up to 60 mph) to the sfc over the west 
half Friday afternoon into early evening; thus, the Marginal Risk 
(category 1 of 5) that SPC has over us. In addition to the 
potentially stronger winds via the convection, some heavy rainfall 
is expected given the robust lift along the front. With PWATs 
generally getting up to around 1.50 inches ahead of the cold front, 
some heavy rainfall in excess of 1 inch could be seen across some 
spots of Upper Michigan; as of the time of this writing, the REFS 
brings up to a 50% chance that over an inch of rainfall will be seen 
between Friday morning and Saturday morning, with the highest 
chances over the west and north central. Looking at the LPMM for the 
REFS, the expected rainfall ranges from a quarter inch to 2+ inches 
over the west and north central, with the Porkies seeing 4+ inches. 
Therefore, while not expected, there could some spots, especially in 
the west, where some ponding of water/flash flood could occur. 
Across the rest of the U.P., expect generally a tenth of an inch up 
to potentially a whole inch of liquid by Saturday morning.

Moving into the rest of the forecast period, expect generally 
pleasant temperatures with highs in the 70s as a somewhat more zonal 
to northwesterly flow sets up across the Upper Great Lakes. While 
some weak sfc ridging generally sets up across the area, some weak 
shortwaves from time to time look to bring additional showers and 
thunderstorms to the area this weekend through next week. With 850mb 
temperatures dropping to around 9 to 10C behind the cold front early 
on Saturday, we may see some lake effect clouds over the northwest 
wind belts early Saturday morning, before warming temperatures bring 
an end to the cloud cover. Looking at just the 0-6 km bulk shear and 
MUCAPE, there is a chance that we could see some stronger storms 
come Sunday, but confidence on this is very low at this time (<5% 
chance). In addition, with a shortwave low on Monday having trended 
further south and now bringing the wrap-around moisture over the 
U.P., we could see at least a wetting rainfall across the area then 
(the NBM shows a 10 to 60% chance for at least a quarter inch of 
rainfall on Monday). By around next Thursday, we could see some lake 
effect clouds return as strong CAA with 850mb temperatures down to 
6C potentially drop across Lake Superior.
